coding_context.description: As the Gender Empowerment Measure increased in value, the tendency decreased for women to place greater emphasis than men on a potential spouse's earning capacity (ranking data)
coding_context.reported_success_quote: Here we attempted to replicate previously reported links between sex differences in mate preferences and country-level measures of gender inequality [...]. Although women preferred mates with good earning capacity more than men did and men preferred physically attractive mates more than women did, we found little evidence that these sex differences were smaller in countries with greater gender equality. Although one analysis suggested that the sex difference in preferences for good earning capacity was smaller in countries with greater gender equality, this effect was not significant when controlling for Galton’s problem or when correcting for multiple comparisons. Collectively, these results provide little support for the social roles account of sex differences in mate preferences.

coding_context.description: Input, Process, and Output Anxiety Scales predict general language learning anxiety
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
In both the initial as well as the replication study, evidence showed
that language learners experience significantly higher levels of output anxiety than
input or process anxiety; nonetheless, these three types of anxiety were found to be
linked to the general concept of language anxiety to different degrees, with process
anxiety depicting the strongest association according to the results of data analysis
in the initial and the replication study.
Although the scales could be characterized as reliable, their componential struc-
ture was found to be not without flaws. Some of the same items of the scales were
labelled as problematic in the Hungarian version of the scales as well as in the English
version. As such, it can be said that these issues are inherent to the items rather than
to their translated versions and thus warrant reconsideration.

coding_context.description: effect of red on attractiveness perceptions
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Results of this meta-analysis showed no effect of red on attractiveness ratings for either perceived attractiveness (mean ratings difference = –0.07, 95% CI [–0.31, 0.16]) or sexual

items.worker_notes: Only assigned unfinished fields n_r and reported_success were examined for completion; original side and replication es/p are unassigned placeholders. Candidate basal-ASR tests on p. 447: overall prenatal DEX effect F(1,70) = 7.520; P = 0.008; light-phase DEX versus CON, pups nested within litter, F(1,28) = 5.963; P = 0.021; dark-phase DEX versus CON, pups nested within litter, F(1,28) = 3.462; P = 0.073. coding_context.description: In this paper, the authors offer insight into a previously documented observation known as the left-digit bias, whereby consumers tend to give greater weight to the left-most digit when comparing two prices. This means, for example, that consumers tend to treat a price difference of $4.00 vs. $2.99 as larger than $4.01 vs. $3.00. The authors’ key claim is that this bias is greater when the prices are presented side-by-side, in a way that makes them easier to compare, than sequentially, on two separate but consecutive screens.
coding_context.reported_success_quote: We find marginally significant support for the authors’ key interaction in both replications. [...] Although the evidence is much weaker than in the original study, we are inclined to believe that the original effect is real.

Newly collected data corroborated Irwin et al.’s (2013) finding that encouragement using the
ambiguous and exclusive pronoun “you” (e.g. “you can do it”) from a virtually present partner
significantly weakened this Köhler effect. Some partial support was found for Irwin et al.’s expla-
nation of this effect. Irwin et al. suggested that when one hears one’s partner say things like “you
can do it!”, that may be interpreted that the partner is him/herself struggling and is to some degree
trying to encourage him/herself. Hence, that partner may not be as superior as previously thought.

items.worker_target_description: Studies 1 & 2 only: meta-analysis of process versus outcome accountability on reinvestment in the initially chosen department (escalating commitment); p.120 right column, explicitly named contrast. We then tested the effect of process versus outcome account- ... ability, which had also been significant in the original study.
items.worker_notes: All three assigned rows provide the identical description naming process versus outcome accountability, and all locate replication Studies 1 & 2 (Meta) on p.120. Each is therefore matched independently to that explicitly named two-experiment contrast; no distinct comparison is inferred from audit_id, row order, or numbers. The p.120 process-versus-no-accountability contrast (d=-0.04, p=.77) and outcome-versus-no-accountability contrast (d=0.03, p=.82) are different comparisons, not assigned by row order. The process-versus-outcome analysis adding the original study (d=-0.30, p=.21) is also excluded because the locator specifies only Studies 1 & 2. Printed metric is d; no further standardisation identity is assumed and no conversion is performed. Analytic N for the selected two-condition contrast is not explicitly supplied. The 353 on p.121 covers all THREE corresponding conditions across both experiments (including no-accountability), not this two-condition contrast. Experiment 1 reports 205 final participants across four conditions and 154 across the three replication conditions; Experiment 2 reports 199 across three conditions. No explicit complete final group counts supporting a sum for the target contrast are printed in the supplied article; no N is derived from df, plot points, manipulation-check denominators, or subtraction. Experiment 1 excludes 15 (5 refusal to be videotaped, 4 wrong questionnaire, 2 uninterpretable answer, 3 suspicious, 1 premature termination); eight nonstudents never entered its original sample. Experiment 2 excludes 16 (10 technical problems, 3 procedure mistakes, 3 disbelief/quit); ten ineligible people never entered its original sample. Original side, reported_success, and unassigned replication fields are placeholders only and were not evaluated.

coding_context.description: Whether holding decision makers accountable for the decision process decreases escalating commitment, while accountability for the decision outcomes increases it.
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
However, as we did
not replicate the original effects in a first experiment, in spite of the fact that our materials and our
procedure resembled the original study as closely as possible, we conducted a second experiment with
an even stronger accountability manipulation as compared to the original study, and with an increased
sample size. Once again, no effects of accountability were found. Taken together, the results of these two
experiments question the robustness of the original findings.

However, as we did
not replicate the original effects in a first experiment, in spite of the fact that our materials and our
procedure resembled the original study as closely as possible, we conducted a second experiment with

sample size. Once again, no effects of accountability were found. Taken together, the results of these two
experiments question the robustness of the original findings.

coding_context.description: Participants who encounter scarcity salience in a prior unrelated context would be more likely to use the provided products in novel but appropriate ways to solve the given task (differences between the scarcity condition and the abundance condition)
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
A chi-square test revealed no significant effect of resource availability on the correctness
of the solutions (X2 (2, N = 319) = 2.224, p = .329). We next conducted a binary logistic
regression analysis to assess the differences between the conditions. The results showed
that there were no significant differences between the scarcity condition (M=27%) and
the abundance condition (M = 29%, B = -.02, [SE] = .06, Wald = .063, p = .802), and
that there was no significant difference between the scarcity condition and the control
condition (M = 36%, B = -.09, [SE] = .06, Wald = 1.90, p = .174.) Furthermore, we
observed no difference between the abundance and control conditions (B = -.07, [SE] =
.06, Wald = 1.2, p = .278). Including careless responders did not qualitatively change
the key study result: there was still no significant difference between the scarcity and
control condition (M = 36%, B = -.10, [SE] = .06, Wald = 2.422, p = .120).

items.worker_target_description: On Track conceptual replication, Table 6 Tobit models for word reading, reading comprehension and spelling, full and reduced samples; row correspondence unresolved.
items.worker_notes:
The p. 18 locator matches PDF p. 18 / printed p. 104, Table 6, visually checked from the rendered PDF. The blank description for audit 65 and generic Early Reading Intervention descriptions for audits 66/67 do not specify outcome or full versus reduced conceptual-replication sample. No row-order or numeric matching used.
Printed Table 6 candidates (Tobit intervention estimate; SE; p; Hedges’ g): word reading full 0.90; 0.45; .047; 0.31, reduced 1.03; 0.48; .031; 0.36. Reading comprehension full 1.19; 0.67; .073; 0.41, reduced 0.94; 0.39; .015; 0.58. Spelling full 1.81; 0.45; .000; 0.46, reduced 2.09; 0.46; .000; 0.54. Each p belongs to the same model as its paired estimate and g. The printed .000 values are preserved as candidates, not changed to bounds. No candidate is assigned to an audit row.
Table 6 does not give analytic N. The Sample section gives 2,170 final students, including 1,687 enrolled in intervention schools, 102 classes across 41 schools. These are study-sample counts, not established target Tobit analytic Ns. Exclusions: students without parental consent; all students at one control school failing to report October pre-assessment. Reduced Tobit analyses additionally exclude intervention students with 50 or fewer sessions (23.3% of intervention students), but no reduced analytic count is printed. No N calculated. Table 5 logistic models give observations 2,106 letter writing, 2,105 phoneme isolation, 2,106 spelling, 2,105 word reading, 2,102 reading comprehension; these separate models cannot establish Table 6 analytic Ns.
Reported success records the authors' overall positive intervention verdict, with smaller effects than the original. It does not assert all Tobit outcomes significant: the authors explicitly note full-sample reading comprehension did not reach .05 (p = .073). Original side unassigned placeholder; original primary source not supplied or inspected.

coding_context.reported_success_quote: Results indicated that the intervention significantly reduced the number of at-risk students by the end of first grade. However, effect sizes in the replication study were reduced compared to the original try-out.

items.worker_notes: The supplied description and p. 3 locator identify the bi-factor replication broadly but do not specify a model contrast, goodness-of-fit test, factor, or item. All three assigned rows have identical target descriptions and locators. Section 3.2 reports several candidate tests; the rows cannot be assigned to them by order or numerical matching. Candidate paired tests, not assigned to any row: content-specific bi-factor versus content-specific model, Δχ2(12) = 206.24, p < .001; content-specific bi-factor versus valence bi-factor, Δχ2(4) = 50.16, p < .001; alternative valence bi-factor versus valence bi-factor, Δχ2(4) = 11.65, p = .020. These are printed chi-square difference tests, not converted effects. Table 1 additionally reports model goodness-of-fit chi-squares (including content-specific bi-factor χ2 = 518.83, df = 75), without model p values. Tables 2 and 3 contain item loadings and factor variance/reliability metrics, respectively; the input does not identify a particular item or factor. No candidate is promoted to the row-specific es or p fields. Candidate model N = 3906 participants, explicitly printed in Table 1, not inferred from df or a recruitment-only total. Participants are adolescents from 13 Netherlands high schools; 13 is a school count, not participant N. Section 3.1 reports 0.5 % missing data, and section 2.3 says missing data was handled through multiple imputation. No additional exclusions are specified in these sections. No N sum or arithmetic is used. Because the requested row-specific test remains unresolved, model N is retained only as a candidate for parent field-scope review. Reported success is the authors’ overall verdict on the described bi-factor replication; it does not resolve the row-specific contrast. Original fields are unassigned placeholders. Supplied primary PDF pages 2–4 were rendered and visually inspected; evidence quotes refer to canonical supplied text.

items.worker_notes: Only assigned n_r and reported_success completed. Original side and replication es/p are unassigned placeholders, not findings of absence. Analytic N derivation: 25 English-speaking + 32 Tseltal-speaking = 57 distinct children (Fig.2), mutually exclusive language groups in the instructed-condition analysis. Methods cross-check: English Ego-to-Geo 13 + Geo-to-Ego 12 = 25; Tseltal Ego-to-Geo 16 + Geo-to-Ego 16 = 32. Repeated egocentric/geocentric and easy/hard measurements are not summed. N is not inferred from df or whole-study recruitment. Reported success is mixed at the Experiment 1 replication-and-extension level: the authors say the replication portion mirrored Haun et al., while added manipulations did not favor the linguistic enculturation account. This is not a separate author verdict on each ANOVA main effect. The instructed-condition outcome is percentage correct, distinct from open-ended strategy classification. Rendered PDF pages 4–7 inspected for layout.
